title: 22. Interview: Scalability
summary: Interview Q&A for Scalability — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Scalability interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Define vertical scaling and horizontal scaling, and give one workload best suited to each.
**Answer:** Vertical scaling (scale up) means adding more CPU, RAM, or faster disks to a single machine — the application code does not change. Horizontal scaling (scale out) means adding more machines and distributing load across them. Vertical scaling is best for workloads that are inherently single-process and stateful, such as a relational database primary or a single Redis instance, where the working set must fit in memory and cross-node coordination would dominate latency. The ceiling is the largest instance your cloud offers, and the box is a single point of failure. Horizontal scaling is best for stateless workloads — web servers, API services, stateless microservices — where any instance can serve any request and adding instances gives near-linear throughput. The ceiling is your budget and operational capacity, not instance size. Real architectures blend both: a vertically-scaled database primary with horizontally-scaled read replicas, fronted by horizontally-scaled stateless web tiers, all behind a load balancer.

**Visual:**
```
Vertical:  [box: 4cpu] -> [box: 8cpu] -> [box: 64cpu]   (ceiling: largest SKU)
Horizontal:[box][box]   -> [box][box][box][box]          (ceiling: $ + ops)
```

### Q2. What does "linear scaling" mean and how do you detect sub-linear scaling?
**Answer:** Linear scaling means throughput grows in proportion to resources added — double the nodes, double the QPS at the same latency. Sub-linear scaling means throughput grows slower than resources — double the nodes, get only 1.3x QPS — because a bottleneck remains. You detect it by plotting throughput against instance count under a sustained load test: a linear system traces a straight 45-degree line; a sub-linear system curves and flattens. The flattening is caused by a shared resource the new nodes still contend on — a database primary, a distributed lock, a connection pool, a single Kafka partition, a network egress limit. The discipline of scalability engineering is to find that shared resource, remove or shard it, and re-run the test until the curve is straight. If you cannot make it straight, you have hit an architectural ceiling — usually the CAP or Amdahl limit — and a redesign is required, not more nodes.

**Visual:**
```
throughput
   ^
   |        linear (good)
   |      /
   |    /         sub-linear (bottleneck)
   |  /         ___________
   |/         /
   +-----------------------> instances
```

### Q3. Why is the first rule of horizontal scaling "make services stateless"?
**Answer:** A stateless service can serve any request on any instance, so a load balancer can freely add, remove, and rebalance instances — that is the foundation of horizontal autoscaling. A stateful service cannot: if instance A holds user 42's session, every request from user 42 must reach instance A (sticky sessions) or the state must be replicated to all instances (expensive and inconsistent). Sticky sessions break autoscaling — you cannot drain instance A without logging out its users — and they concentrate load unevenly. State replication adds latency and complexity. The fix is to externalize state to a dedicated store: session state to Redis, file uploads to S3, shared mutable data to a database. Then the compute tier becomes stateless and can be cloned freely. The trade-off is that every request now pays a network hop to the state store, which is why a co-located in-process cache (with cache-aside invalidation) is often added back. The pattern is: stateless compute, externalized state, optional per-instance cache for read-heavy workloads.

**Visual:**
```
Stateful (bad for horizontal scale):
   LB -> [node A (sess 42)] [node B (sess 7)]
   user 42 must hit node A -> cannot drain A -> cannot autoscale freely

Stateless (good):
   LB -> [node 1] [node 2] [node N]    (any can serve any request)
            \      |      /
             \     |     /
            [ Redis / S3 / DB ]   <-- state lives here
```

### Q4. Explain the scalability staircase and why the order matters.
**Answer:** The scalability staircase is the order in which tiers saturate as load grows: load balancer → web tier → app tier → cache → database primary (writes) → database replicas (reads) → network egress. You scale whichever tier is currently the bottleneck; scaling a non-bottleneck tier wastes money. The classic mistake is adding 50 web nodes when the single database primary is saturated — throughput does not improve because the DB is still the limit, and you have just spent 50 nodes' worth of money for nothing. The correct sequence is: measure per-tier saturation (CPU, connection pool, disk I/O, network); identify the first tier past ~70% utilization; scale that tier; re-measure; the bottleneck will move to the next tier; repeat. The order matters because each tier has a different cost and ceiling — adding web nodes is cheap (dollars), sharding a database is expensive (months of engineering), and upgrading a network pipe may require a contract renegotiation. The staircase tells you which lever to pull next.

**Visual:**
```
traffic ->
  [LB]  -> [web] -> [app] -> [cache] -> [DB primary (W)] -> [DB replicas (R)]
   ^                                              ^
   |                                              |
  scales first                            scales last, hardest
  (cheap, stateless)                     (sharding, replicas, denormalize)
```

### Q5. How did Netflix's move from data centers to AWS exemplify vertical-to-horizontal scaling?
**Answer:** In their owned data centers, Netflix ran on vertically-scaled big-iron Oracle databases and large monolithic servers. They hit two walls: traffic grew faster than they could procure and rack hardware (procurement took weeks), and a single DC was a single point of failure. Moving to AWS was fundamentally a move from vertical to horizontal scaling. Instead of buying one bigger box, Netflix ran hundreds of smaller EC2 instances in autoscaling groups. Stateless web/API tiers autoscale on CPU; stateful tiers (Cassandra, EVCache) are sharded across many instances; encoding workloads autoscale on queue depth. The benefit was not just capacity — it was resilience: losing an instance became a non-event handled by the autoscaler, not a 3 a.m. page. The cost was operational complexity, which Netflix answered with chaos engineering (the Simian Army) to verify the horizontally-scaled system actually survived failures. The lesson: horizontal scaling is not just "more boxes," it is a redesign of how the system handles failure, deployment, and state.

**Visual:**
```
2008 (vertical, DC):       [ big-iron Oracle ]  +  [ few large servers ]
                              ^                       ^
                              | single point of       | slow procurement
                              | failure               |
                              v                       v
2012 (horizontal, AWS):    [ N small EC2 in ASG ] + [ Cassandra cluster ]
                            + [ EVCache sharded ]   + [ Chaos Monkey ]
```

### Q6. What is sharding, and what trade-offs does it introduce?
**Answer:** Sharding is horizontal scaling for stateful data: the dataset is partitioned across multiple nodes by a shard key, so each node owns a slice of the data and serves only the requests routed to it. The benefit is that both storage and write throughput scale with the number of shards — add shards, get more capacity. The trade-offs are substantial. First, **cross-shard operations are expensive or impossible**: a query that joins data on shard A with data on shard B requires a scatter-gather, and transactions across shards require two-phase commit or sagas. Second, the **shard key choice is sticky**: a poor choice (e.g., sharding users by `created_at`) creates hot shards; a good choice (e.g., `user_id`) spreads load evenly but limits query patterns. Third, **resharding is painful**: moving data between shards without downtime requires dual-writing or log shipping, and is the kind of migration teams put off for years. Fourth, **operational complexity rises**: backups, schema migrations, and replication all become per-shard. Sharding is the right answer when the largest single primary cannot keep up, but it should be deferred as long as possible — premature sharding is a classic mistake.

**Visual:**
```
Shard key: user_id mod 4

  user 1, 5, 9   ->  [ Shard 0 ]
  user 2, 6, 10  ->  [ Shard 1 ]
  user 3, 7, 11  ->  [ Shard 2 ]
  user 4, 8, 12  ->  [ Shard 3 ]

Cross-shard query:  SELECT * WHERE country = 'US'
   -> scatter to all 4 shards -> gather -> merge   (expensive)
```

### Q7. Why does autoscaling always lag the load, and how do you mitigate that?
**Answer:** Reactive autoscalers trigger on past metrics — they add capacity after CPU has already spiked, not before. Even with a 60-second metric window and a 30-second cooldown, a 10x viral spike will overload the fleet for 2–5 minutes before new nodes warm up, and warm-up itself takes another minute or two (JIT compilation, cache priming, connection pool ramp). The result is degraded latency or errors during the lag window. Mitigations: (1) **warm spare capacity** — always run 20–30% above current need so a 1.5x spike is absorbed without scaling; (2) **predictive scaling** — use historical patterns (e.g., weekday morning ramp) to pre-scale before the spike; (3) **scheduled scaling** — for known events (product launch, Prime Day), pre-scale to expected peak; (4) **graceful degradation** — shed low-priority work (batch jobs, analytics) to free capacity for user-facing requests; (5) **rate limiting** — reject excess load at the edge with a 429 rather than letting it saturate the fleet. The architectural lesson: autoscaling is not a substitute for headroom; it is a way to slowly trade cost for capacity between known load patterns.

**Visual:**
```
load
 ^
 |     /  actual load (10x spike)
 |    /
 |---/ ..........................  warm spare + autoscaled capacity
 |  /                            (lags by 2-5 min)
 | /
 +--------------------------------> time
       ^spike  ^overload window  ^autoscaler catches up
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your API's p99 latency doubled after traffic grew 3x, but CPU on every instance is at 40%. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Low CPU but high latency points to a non-CPU bottleneck — most likely a downstream resource the web tier is waiting on. The four usual suspects: (1) **database connection pool exhaustion** — instances spend time waiting for a free connection; check pool utilization and `wait_time_ms`. (2) **A saturated downstream service or cache** — Redis hit rate dropped, or a downstream API's queue is backing up; check cache hit ratio and downstream p99. (3) **Network I/O** — instances are bandwidth-limited or hitting a per-connection throttle; check network bytes per instance. (4) **Lock contention** — a single mutex is serializing requests even though CPU is idle; check thread dumps. The diagnostic order: instrument the request path with per-hop latency (OpenTelemetry / distributed tracing), find the hop whose duration grew, and that is the bottleneck. The fix depends on which it is — grow the connection pool, add cache capacity, shard the downstream, or refactor the lock. Adding web instances will not help, because CPU is not the limit — that is the trap of scaling a non-bottleneck tier.

**Visual:**
```
[web cpu 40%]  --- wait ---> [DB conn pool: full]
[web cpu 40%]  --- wait ---> [Redis: 60% hit rate, was 95%]
[web cpu 40%]  --- wait ---> [downstream svc: queue depth 10k]

Diagnosis: trace each request; the slow hop is the bottleneck.
```

### Q2. You run a single Postgres primary handling 5K writes/sec. The team wants to scale to 20K writes/sec. Walk through your options.
**Answer:** First, check whether the bottleneck is CPU, disk IOPS, or WAL throughput — the answer changes the path. Assuming the primary is genuinely at its ceiling, the options in order of preference: (1) **vertical scale** — move to a larger instance with more CPU, faster NVMe, higher IOPS; this buys time but has a hard ceiling, and the largest RDS instance is expensive. (2) **Offload reads** — if a large fraction of the load is reads, add read replicas; this does not help writes but is often the cheapest win. (3) **Partition the data** — Postgres native partitioning by a hot column (e.g., `created_at` month) can reduce per-index size and improve cache hit rate without changing the logical schema much. (4) **Shard the writes** — split the dataset across multiple primaries by a shard key (e.g., `tenant_id`); this is the only path to 20K writes/sec sustained and is a multi-month migration. (5) **Offload writes to a queue** — for non-ACID writes (analytics, logs, telemetry), push to Kafka and consume with batch writers; this decouples write rate from primary capacity. The right answer is usually a combination: vertical scale immediately, partition in the next quarter, and design the sharding path before you actually need it.

**Visual:**
```
5K writes/s -> [single Postgres primary, CPU 90%]
   |
   +--> immediate:  vertical scale (larger instance)
   +--> 1-2 weeks:  read replicas for read load
   +--> 1-3 months: partition by tenant_id or created_at
   +--> 6 months:   shard across N primaries by tenant_id  (target: 20K W/s)
   +--> parallel:   move analytics writes to Kafka + batch consumer
```

### Q3. Your startup's monolith scales to ~500 QPS and then falls over. The team proposes "rewrite to microservices." Critique.
**Answer:** The proposal conflates a scaling problem with an architectural style. Microservices are an organizational scaling pattern — they let multiple teams deploy independently — but they do not inherently make a system handle more QPS. A 500-QPS ceiling on a monolith is almost always a single-tier bottleneck, not a "monolith" problem. Diagnose first: is the limit the web tier (CPU), the database primary (writes), the cache (hit rate), or the network? If the database primary is the limit, microservices will not help — you will just have N services all hammering the same primary. If the web tier is the limit, vertical scaling or a stateless horizontal web tier behind a load balancer fixes it in days, not months. The right move is to extract one well-bounded service at a time using the strangler-fig pattern, only when there is a concrete reason (independent scaling, independent deploy, team boundary). A full microservices rewrite of a working monolith is a 12-month project with a high failure rate; it should be the last resort, not the first.

**Visual:**
```
Monolith at 500 QPS:
   [ web + app + DB-primary ]   <-- find the bottleneck tier
                |
   +--> if DB-primary is limit: microservices will NOT help (still 1 primary)
   +--> if web is limit:        add LB + N stateless web nodes  (days)
   +--> if cache hit rate:      add Redis tier                  (days)
   +--> only extract services when there is a real team/scale reason
```

### Q4. You run a stateful service on 3 nodes. Traffic doubles every 6 months. When do you shard, and how do you avoid painful resharding later?
**Answer:** Shard when the largest single node cannot keep up at peak even after vertical scaling to the maximum instance size — not before. Premature sharding adds operational complexity for no benefit. To avoid painful resharding later, choose a shard key that distributes load evenly and choose a shard count with significant headroom — if your math says you need 4 shards today, deploy 16 or 32 with most of them empty, so the next 18 months of growth is absorbed by filling existing shards rather than adding new ones. Use **consistent hashing** so that adding or removing a shard moves only ~1/N of the keys, not all of them. Plan for **online resharding** from day one — dual-write or log-shipping between old and new shard layouts so you can migrate without downtime. Finally, instrument per-shard load carefully; an unbalanced shard (a "hot shard") will saturate long before the others, and you need to detect it early so you can split it. Cassandra, Redis Cluster, and DynamoDB all use variations of this pattern.

**Visual:**
```
Today: 4 shards needed.
   Deploy 16 shards (most empty) -- absorb 18 months of growth.

   [0][1][2][3][.][.][.][.][.][.][.][.][.][.][.][.]   consistent hash ring
                              ^
                              | add new shard here moves only 1/16 of keys
```

### Q5. A viral product launch doubled traffic in 10 minutes. Autoscaling did not save you. Postmortem the design.
**Answer:** The root cause is autoscaling lag combined with insufficient headroom — the architecture was sized for steady-state, not for spikes. The postmortem should call out: (1) **no warm spare** — the fleet ran at 70% CPU pre-spike, leaving no room to absorb even a 1.5x jump while the autoscaler warmed up; (2) **autoscaler too slow** — 60-second metric window plus 60-second cooldown plus 90-second instance boot means 3–4 minutes before new capacity is live, but the spike doubled load in 10 minutes; (3) **no graceful degradation** — the system tried to serve every request at full quality, so it fell over instead of shedding load. Design fixes: run with 30–40% headroom as a permanent policy; use **scheduled scaling** to pre-scale for known launches; implement **rate limiting at the edge** with a 429 once load exceeds 1.5x the fleet's safe capacity; implement **priority-based load shedding** so user-facing requests survive while batch jobs pause; consider **predictive scaling** based on historical patterns. The deeper lesson: autoscaling optimizes cost between known patterns, it does not protect against spikes — headroom and shedding do.

**Visual:**
```
load      /
        /  (2x in 10 min)
      /
    /.............. fleet capacity (no headroom, autoscaler too slow)
  /    ^^^^ overload window: 4-6 min
 +------------------> time
   spike  autoscaler catches up

Fixes: warm spare 30%, scheduled pre-scale, edge rate limit, load shedding.
```

### Q6. You are designing a globally-distributed chat app expected to reach 1B users. Where do you scale vertically vs horizontally, and why?
**Answer:** Compute tiers (the connection-handling frontend, the message-routing layer) scale horizontally — they are stateless or near-stateless and benefit from geographic distribution. The frontend WebSocket servers run in every region, fronted by a geo-DNS that routes users to the nearest region. The message router shards by conversation id so messages within a conversation always hit the same shard. Storage tiers are mixed: the **hot message store** (last 30 days per conversation) is horizontally sharded Cassandra or DynamoDB, partitioned by conversation id, with replicas in each region; the **cold archive** (older messages) is in cheaper object storage (S3) and is essentially infinitely scalable by virtue of being a managed service. Vertically scaled components are rare but specific: a **single Redis primary per region** for ephemeral presence state (who is online) — one big box outperforms a cluster for the in-memory working set, and presence is region-local. The pattern: horizontally scale the global, partitionable, latency-sensitive tiers; vertically scale the small, region-local, working-set-bound tiers; defer sharding until you actually need it.

**Visual:**
```
Geo-DNS -> [ Region US ] [ Region EU ] [ Region AP ]
              |              |              |
            [ WS x N ]    [ WS x N ]    [ WS x N ]    <-- horizontal
              |              |              |
            [ Router x M, sharded by conversation id ] <-- horizontal
              |              |              |
            [ Redis primary (vert)  ]  <-- presence, region-local
            [ Cassandra shards (horiz) ] <-- hot messages, sharded by conv id
            [ S3 cold archive ]           <-- managed, infinite
```

### Q7. Your Cassandra cluster has a hot shard — one node is at 90% CPU while others are at 30%. Diagnose and fix.
**Answer:** A hot shard means the partition key is unevenly distributed, concentrating load on one node. Common causes: (1) **poor partition key choice** — e.g., partitioning by `country` when 80% of users are in the US, so the US partition is huge and lives on one node; (2) **time-series key without bucketing** — all current-day writes hit the same partition; (3) **a single high-cardinality hot entity** — one celebrity's timeline generates the bulk of the traffic. Diagnose by querying `system.size_estimates` and per-node CPU/disk metrics — the imbalance will be obvious. Fixes: (1) **composite partition key** — add a bucketing column, e.g., `(country, user_id_bucket)` so the US partition splits across multiple nodes; (2) **time bucketing** — partition by `(date, hour)` instead of `date` so writes spread across the ring; (3) **separate hot tenants** — move the celebrity to a dedicated keyspace or a different replication factor. The deeper lesson: in a distributed store, the partition key is the most important schema decision, and you must reason about its cardinality and skew before deploying — fixing it later requires a data migration.

**Visual:**
```
Before (hot shard):
  partition by country:
    [US=80% load] [UK=5%] [DE=3%] [other=12%]
    ^^^ hot node at 90% CPU

After (bucketed):
  partition by (country, user_id_bucket):
    [US-b0] [US-b1] [US-b2] [US-b3] [UK-b0..3] ...
    each ~20% load -> evenly distributed across ring
```
